football_evidence.question: Can Kentucky’s pass rush get to Jared Curtis?
football_evidence.assessment: Some measured evidence supports EdgeDesk’s lean toward Kentucky, and its own breakdown accounts for about 2.2 of the 4.0 points, but not the full gap. It is a research question, not a bet.
supporting: When Vanderbilt has the ball (big plays on the ground): Vanderbilt’s offense turns 5.2% of its runs into explosive gains, and Kentucky’s defense gives up explosive gains on 3.6% of opponent runs (FBS average 6.6%).

contradicting: When Kentucky has the ball (pass protection against the pass rush): Kentucky’s offense has allowed a sack on 7.1% of its dropbacks, and Vanderbilt’s defense sacks the quarterback on 6.2% of opponent dropbacks (FBS average 5.6%).
When Vanderbilt has the ball (third down): Vanderbilt’s offense converts 43.0% of its third downs, and Kentucky’s defense allows opponents to convert 49.1% of their third downs (FBS average 39.7%).
In his last two games (LSU and Oklahoma), Minchey averaged 6.1 yards per attempt, against 8.2 in his five games before that.
